Eastern Cape Drought

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Eastern Cape is in the grips of one of the worst droughts in living memory...

Unique Selling Point:
We take a trip to the Western parts of the Eastern Cape where the current drought has taken its toll on the humans, the wildlife and agriculture in the region. The area has had no rain for more than 5 years. The Eastern Cape straddles an area of 16 857 million hectares with a population of 6.5 million, mostly rural. This is the poorest of the nine provinces and the knock-on effect of the drought is having disastrous consequences. This week the Chris Hani District Municipality started imposing water rationing as dam levels are simply too low, Many smaller towns like Butterworth have been faced with a Day Zero scenario months ago.

Summary:
The Eastern Cape is said to experience the worst drought in living memory. And although some rain (below average) has fallen in the Eastern part of the province the Western region has had no relief. The Chris Hani District municipality has announced water rationing and many smaller towns and villages are relying on borehole water as dams are drying up. Organisations like Gift of the Givers are working tirelessly to gift water to the desperate regions, but its simply not enough and they cannot keep up with the demand. On top of that Climate and water experts say that there's no real relief on its way. The entire province is just said to become hotter and dryer in the future. The continued use of underground water sources is not sustainable as many farmers have reported their boreholes and windpumps drying up. The biggest concern for the province is that the Eastern Cape has by far the largest numbers of livestock in the country. Without water, agriculture cannot continue as normal, which affects the entire economy of the region, but also has a bigger ripple effect on the country as a whole.

According to SA Statistics 2017, 24% of the country’s cattle, 38% of the goats, 29% of all the sheep within South Africa, are farmed in the Eastern Cape. Approximately one third of the Province is extremely/severely dry, with one third being moderately dry and one third being near normal.

This drought in these areas is affecting about 1 440 commercial farmers, 8 700 smallholder farmers and about 55 000 subsistence farmers. These farmers collectively support in the region of 405 200 direct dependents, by means of primary agriculture.

Further information:
Agri Eastern Cape President, Dough Stern, says the severe drought has crippled farmers for five consecutive years. They have now reached a breaking point. According to him, the whole province is buckling under these conditions with the western part of the Eastern Cape which has been greatly affected. In the eastern part of the province below average rainfall brought some relief. The situation is dire, says Stern.

Based on the official report from the EC Department of Rural Development and Agrarian Reform, the following Districts and local Municipalities within the Province have been assessed as extremely and severely dry, expressed in percentages as follows:

Sarah Baartman District 57,6 % with the Blue Crane Route Municipality at 77 % and the Dr Beyers Naude at LM at 65 %;
Amatole District 40,1% with the Raymond Mhlaba LM at 85%;
Chris Hani District 28,9% with the Inxuba Yethemba LM at 68%.

Dam levels within the Districts indicate that within the three districts declared, the average number of major dam levels that have declined over the last twelve months are as follows:

Sarah Baartman District and the Nelson Mandela Bay Metro 5 out of a total of 10 dams with 6 dams below 50%;
Amatole District 12 out of a total of 14 dams with 8 dams below 50%;
Chris Hani District 11 out of a total of 14 dams with 6 dams below 50%.

According to estimates, livestock numbers decreased over the previous 12 months as follows: cattle by 55 000, sheep by 180 000 and goats by 72 000.

With a third of the province in a critical position, more than 1 million cattle, 2.1 million sheep and 600 000 goats face an uncertain future.

At least 30 million Rands worth of feed is going to be needed daily to prevent these animals from dying or having to be slaughtered.

Press Release:


The Eastern Cape: Dry Dams and Empty Boreholes
From Butterworth to Graaff-Reinet, it’s been five long years without sufficient rainfall in crucial parts of the Eastern Cape. No rain meant no water and after prolonged periods - dry dams, empty boreholes and communities left destitute. Farms have become arid and livestock is dying out. This week, there was a glimmer of hope with some much-needed rainfall – but will this be enough to pull the province out of this ongoing drought?
Producer: Stenette Groskopf | Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


EC Drought 2020 SCRIPT



Mzikayise Luwalala
Every morning I have to feed my goats that are staying here. Because even if I take them out to go and graze … there’s no food...


Eastern Cape emerging farmer, Mzikayise Luwalala’s sheep and goats are slowly starving to death.
Mzikayise Luwalala
You know we have been feeding since May till now, as you can see they are even eating the pampers...


He’s struggling to keep up and for the past few months he has had stock losses... almost on a daily basis.
Mzikayise Luwalala
I have to go and throw them away during the night time so that people cannot see and laugh at me. Because this situation really is embarrassing. Time and again you’re taking your goats and your sheep and throw it away. It’s dead.
LINK
The Eastern Cape is known for its rolling green hills but for more than four years now the rain has stayed away. 40 to 50% of the province is experiencing severe to extreme drought everyone is suffering - from the big towns to the small villages.
V/o
The province is said to have the largest numbers of livestock in the country, with about 4,000 commercial farmers, 30,000 small-scale farmers and 500,000 subsistence farmers.
Doug Stern
The significance of agriculture in the Eastern Cape is huge because we must understand that this province is primarily dependent on agriculture and tourism to a lesser extent.
V/O
Doug Stern farms in the Sarah Baartman District near the town of Graaff Reinett, which is one of the hardest hit regions in the province. He is also the president of Agri EC.
Doug Stern
Records will tell us that this is the worst drought since our records have been kept - that’s about 100 years. And what has made it worse is the fact that it’s been five consecutive years, and last year we only had about 35% of our average rainfall.
V/O
Once again the Sarah Baartman-, Amatole -, and Chris Hani Districts have been declared Drought Disaster Areas… - When you look at the veld some of the hardy shrubs and trees appear to be green, but it is the grass - or lack thereof - that reveals the truth...



Noluthando
This place is like a desert, there is no water, there are no dams, there aren’t any tree for the livestock to graze on ,they solely depend on grass. It’s tough if you don’t have money.
V/O
Noluthando Mtombeni runs the local traditional farmers’ co-op in the rural town of Whittlesea about 50kms south of Komani.

Noluthando
Farmers in Whittlesea are very much affected because every morning I get reports from farmers saying they have lost three cows , they have lost twelve or twenty- five sheep...


v/O
This morning is no different.. Three sheep are dead and the farmer is encouraging the lambs to hold one just a little longer...
Mzikayise Luwalala
I think this is the fourth or the 5th year we’ve been struggling in this community of Sada. We don’t know really. We are suffering. We don’t know whether to stop keeping the livestock and just go to Cape Town maybe and work there.
V/O
On top of loadshedding, most towns are experiencing some form of water rationing and many residents only get water for an hour or two, and not necessarily every day. Throughout the province local governance has broken down - services like refuse collection, and cleaning up, and delivering water tankers to assist, are non-existent.
Doug Stern
The municipalities are guilty of not performing their work properly. They knew what was coming and they have not been able to look after their infrastructures of their various municipalities.
Ken Clark
We’re in an advanced stage of collapse and as far as I’m concerned urgent action is required to save our towns.
V/O
In Queenstown - now Komani - prominent businessman, and CEO of Twizza, Kenneth Clark has tried various avenues to remedy the town’s municipal woes.
Ken Clark
It’s an absolute crisis. And to deny it’s a crisis is being foolhardy. And you know like I say to most people, the first job of fixing a problem is understanding and admitting that you have a problem.
LINK
Unfortunately this has become a common sight since the drought has worsened in the Eastern Cape. Cows get so desperate for food that they eat plastic. Most of them die but a lucky few get saved.


V/O
The animals scavenge for scraps between the rubbish and in the process ingest some of the waste, including the plastic. And the people let them eat because at least it keeps their stomachs full.

This cow was thought to be pregnant, but instead the veterinarian removed 9 kilograms of plastic from its gut.
V/O
Just about a kilometre up the road… more victims of the drought...
LINK
Trust that on the day we come to the Eastern Cape to do a story on the drought the heavens open up and it is pouring with rain. But we can’t get excited because not even this rain that we see here today is going to be nearly enough for the people that are suffering here.
Dylan Fetting
It’s raining for the first time in a month now, I think we last had 3mls about three weeks ago. And if you drive on that road about half an hour later it’s already dry.
V/O
Dylan Fetting runs the local butchery in Fort Beaufort in the Amatole District, whilst his father and brother are based on the family farm.
Dylan Fetting
It’s been our driest year, according to some farmers records, since 1922. So I really don’t think that 20mls, 30mls 50mls, even 100mls is going to break it. We need 100mls or more and then follow-up rains after that is really what is key.
V/O
The drought is putting pressure on the entire economy of the province. Like the farmers, businesses are directly impacted… To keep the butchery running they’ve had to import animals from other provinces...
Dylan Fetting
That’s obviously at an increased cost to the butcher and therefore increased cost to your end consumer.
LINK
This is Bonkolo Dam just outside of Komani - once the lifeline for the town it is now bone dry just like many dams across the province.
V/O
And the town is feeling the effects of the drought. Water shortages in Komani - have impacted production at the local plant of the province’s soft drink giant, Twizza. And Chief Operations Officer, Lisle Clarke says that affects the entire community.
Lisle Clarke
I think the most remarkable impact was now over our peak season in Dec and Jan where almost 50% of our business that we’d service out of this plant we had to service out of other plants.
V/O
This means that often stock has to be imported from their Middleburg branch in Mpumalanga to go to Eastern Cape Customers.
Lisle Clarke
You’re travelling twice the distance to get your product to the customer and meet their demand, so it’s really double the cost. You’re just about breaking even to get it there.
V/O
Other businesses are facing challenges too. Some 300 kms to the South West lies Shamwari Private Game Reserve - one of the Eastern Cape’s crown jewels. Here too the hardy thorn trees are still green but the rest of the vegetation is all but gone.
Joe Cloete
We manage the water situation now on a daily basis and sometimes even on a half-daily basis. We’re totally reliant on rainfall water.
V/O
General Manager, Joe Cloete took us on a quick tour and down to the Bushmans river, which provides most of the drinking water for the animals. It has been reduced to a couple of large pools - overcrowded with hippos.
Joe Cloete
We’re already feeding hippos. We may have to start feeding some of the other major herbivores that are struggling, like rhino and buffalo. We may have to try and catch animals and move them to areas where there is water and where there is adequate grazing. But we’ve got to be hopeful. The long-term forecast indicates that there should be some rain in the next couple of months. We’ve only got a couple of months left. We can’t really hang out much longer than that.
V/O
As with livestock farming, the carrying capacity of the land is crucial. Land managers need to be clear on how many animals a specific piece of land can sustain. Dr John O’Brien is the ecologist on the reserve.
Dr John O’Brien
In terms of our carrying capacity we try and manage for the worst case scenario. Now the worst case scenario is now.
However, if the rains don’t come before, let’s call it Feb March we’re not going to get a growth season in the grass over winter. It’s actually going to have a detrimental effect where we will find animal populations start dropping...
V/O
And of course, much to everyone’s delight some rain has fallen this week. Some rivers are flowing for the first time in many months...
UPSOUND
Ons wou kom kyk het hoe loop die rivier!
V/o
Social media is flooded with photos and videos of people enjoying the rain, and there is an air of hope… but everyone agrees that they need a lot more before this drought is officially history...
Doug Stern
What one must understand is the vegetation is so damaged, it’s going to take a lot of rain to be able to resuscitate the root systems of these plants. And we’re going to have to manage our veld very very sensitively to allow the veld to recover properly.
V/O
Whether this rain can be counted as significant or not, the province is still in desperate need of assistance from government. In November last year The Eastern Cape Department of Rural Development and Agrarian Reform pledged R74 million to farmers but no-one we spoke to has any knowledge of where this money has been spent. According to Agri EC there has been almost no assistance from National Government to date, despite being declared a drought disaster area. But Minister of Human Settlements, Water and Sanitation, Lindiwe Sisulu promised “some funding” during her visit to East London a few days ago.
Mzikayise Luwalala
We need water. We need government to at least try and help us. Not this thing, if they say they are going to help us you find one bale for the whole village. How we’re going to share one lucern bale? You know these people they’re just playing with us man... I mean we need something urgent to be done. We cannot be like this all the time. How can a person survive, man?




PROMO 1 11”
Dry dams and dry boreholes - much of the Eastern Cape is crippled by an intense multi-year drought. And despite widespread rainfall earlier this week, the community is crying for help.
PROMO 2 11”
The Eastern Cape is in the grips of a severe drought and even though some rain came this week, the people of the province are cautious. Is the end of the drought in sight?
PROMO 3 11”
The Eastern Cape is thirsty and not even the recent rain is enough to revive the veld. For how long can communities survive the gruelling drought with minimal assistance from Government.

Doug Stern The municipalities are guilty of not performing their work properly. They knew what was coming and they have not been able to look after their infrastructures of their various municipalities. Ken Clark We’re in an advanced stage of collapse and as far as I’m concerned urgent action is required to save our towns. V/O In Queenstown - now Komani - prominent businessman, and CEO of Twizza, Kenneth Clark has tried various avenues to remedy the town’s municipal woes. Ken Clark It’s an absolute crisis. And to deny it’s a crisis is being foolhardy. And you know like I say to most people, the first job of fixing a problem is understanding and admitting that you have a problem. LINK Unfortunately this has become a common sight since the drought has worsened in the Eastern Cape. Cows get so desperate for food that they eat plastic. Most of them die but a lucky few get saved. V/O The animals scavenge for scraps between the rubbish and in the process ingest some of the waste, including the plastic. And the people let them eat because at least it keeps their stomachs full. This cow was thought to be pregnant, but instead the veterinarian removed 9 kilograms of plastic from its gut. V/O Just about a kilometre up the road… more victims of the drought... LINK Trust that on the day we come to the Eastern Cape to do a story on the drought the heavens open up and it is pouring with rain. But we can’t get excited because not even this rain that we see here today is going to be nearly enough for the people that are suffering here. Dylan Fetting It’s raining for the first time in a month now, I think we last had 3mls about three weeks ago. And if you drive on that road about half an hour later it’s already dry. V/O Dylan Fetting runs the local butchery in Fort Beaufort in the Amatole District, whilst his father and brother are based on the family farm. Dylan Fetting It’s been our driest year, according to some farmers records, since 1922. So I really don’t think that 20mls, 30mls 50mls, even 100mls is going to break it. We need 100mls or more and then follow-up rains after that is really what is key. V/O The drought is putting pressure on the entire economy of the province. Like the farmers, businesses are directly impacted… To keep the butchery running they’ve had to import animals from other provinces... Dylan Fetting That’s obviously at an increased cost to the butcher and therefore increased cost to your end consumer. LINK This is Bonkolo Dam just outside of Komani - once the lifeline for the town it is now bone dry just like many dams across the province. V/O And the town is feeling the effects of the drought. Water shortages in Komani - have impacted production at the local plant of the province’s soft drink giant, Twizza. And Chief Operations Officer, Lisle Clarke says that affects the entire community. Lisle Clarke I think the most remarkable impact was now over our peak season in Dec and Jan where almost 50% of our business that we’d service out of this plant we had to service out of other plants. V/O This means that often stock has to be imported from their Middleburg branch in Mpumalanga to go to Eastern Cape Customers. Lisle Clarke You’re travelling twice the distance to get your product to the customer and meet their demand, so it’s really double the cost. You’re just about breaking even to get it there. V/O Other businesses are facing challenges too. Some 300 kms to the South West lies Shamwari Private Game Reserve - one of the Eastern Cape’s crown jewels. Here too the hardy thorn trees are still green but the rest of the vegetation is all but gone. Joe Cloete We manage the water situation now on a daily basis and sometimes even on a half-daily basis. We’re totally reliant on rainfall water. V/O General Manager, Joe Cloete took us on a quick tour and down to the Bushmans river, which provides most of the drinking water for the animals. It has been reduced to a couple of large pools - overcrowded with hippos. Joe Cloete We’re already feeding hippos. We may have to start feeding some of the other major herbivores that are struggling, like rhino and buffalo. We may have to try and catch animals and move them to areas where there is water and where there is adequate grazing. But we’ve got to be hopeful. The long-term forecast indicates that there should be some rain in the next couple of months. We’ve only got a couple of months left. We can’t really hang out much longer than that. V/O As with livestock farming, the carrying capacity of the land is crucial. Land managers need to be clear on how many animals a specific piece of land can sustain. Dr John O’Brien is the ecologist on the reserve. Dr John O’Brien In terms of our carrying capacity we try and manage for the worst case scenario. Now the worst case scenario is now. However, if the rains don’t come before, let’s call it Feb March we’re not going to get a growth season in the grass over winter. It’s actually going to have a detrimental effect where we will find animal populations start dropping... V/O And of course, much to everyone’s delight some rain has fallen this week. Some rivers are flowing for the first time in many months... UPSOUND Ons wou kom kyk het hoe loop die rivier! V/o Social media is flooded with photos and videos of people enjoying the rain, and there is an air of hope… but everyone agrees that they need a lot more before this drought is officially history... Doug Stern What one must understand is the vegetation is so damaged, it’s going to take a lot of rain to be able to resuscitate the root systems of these plants. And we’re going to have to manage our veld very very sensitively to allow the veld to recover properly. V/O Whether this rain can be counted as significant or not, the province is still in desperate need of assistance from government. In November last year The Eastern Cape Department of Rural Development and Agrarian Reform pledged R74 million to farmers but no-one we spoke to has any knowledge of where this money has been spent. According to Agri EC there has been almost no assistance from National Government to date, despite being declared a drought disaster area. But Minister of Human Settlements, Water and Sanitation, Lindiwe Sisulu promised “some funding” during her visit to East London a few days ago. Mzikayise Luwalala We need water. We need government to at least try and help us. Not this thing, if they say they are going to help us you find one bale for the whole village. How we’re going to share one lucern bale? You know these people they’re just playing with us man... I mean we need something urgent to be done. We cannot be like this all the time. How can a person survive, man? PROMO 1 11” Dry dams and dry boreholes - much of the Eastern Cape is crippled by an intense multi-year drought. And despite widespread rainfall earlier this week, the community is crying for help. PROMO 2 11” The Eastern Cape is in the grips of a severe drought and even though some rain came this week, the people of the province are cautious. Is the end of the drought in sight? PROMO 3 11” The Eastern Cape is thirsty and not even the recent rain is enough to revive the veld. For how long can communities survive the gruelling drought with minimal assistance from Government.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The Eastern Cape is in the grips of one of the worst droughts in living memory...
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We take a trip to the Western parts of the Eastern Cape where the current drought has taken its toll on the humans, the wildlife and agriculture in the region. The area has had no rain for more than 5 years. The Eastern Cape straddles an area of 16 857 million hectares with a population of 6.5 million, mostly rural. This is the poorest of the nine provinces and the knock-on effect of the drought is having disastrous consequences. This week the Chris Hani District Municipality started imposing water rationing as dam levels are simply too low, Many smaller towns like Butterworth have been faced with a Day Zero scenario months ago.
metadata.Summary: The Eastern Cape is said to experience the worst drought in living memory. And although some rain (below average) has fallen in the Eastern part of the province the Western region has had no relief. The Chris Hani District municipality has announced water rationing and many smaller towns and villages are relying on borehole water as dams are drying up. Organisations like Gift of the Givers are working tirelessly to gift water to the desperate regions, but its simply not enough and they cannot keep up with the demand. On top of that Climate and water experts say that there's no real relief on its way. The entire province is just said to become hotter and dryer in the future. The continued use of underground water sources is not sustainable as many farmers have reported their boreholes and windpumps drying up. The biggest concern for the province is that the Eastern Cape has by far the largest numbers of livestock in the country. Without water, agriculture cannot continue as normal, which affects the entire economy of the region, but also has a bigger ripple effect on the country as a whole. According to SA Statistics 2017, 24% of the country’s cattle, 38% of the goats, 29% of all the sheep within South Africa, are farmed in the Eastern Cape. Approximately one third of the Province is extremely/severely dry, with one third being moderately dry and one third being near normal. This drought in these areas is affecting about 1 440 commercial farmers, 8 700 smallholder farmers and about 55 000 subsistence farmers. These farmers collectively support in the region of 405 200 direct dependents, by means of primary agriculture.
metadata.Further information: Agri Eastern Cape President, Dough Stern, says the severe drought has crippled farmers for five consecutive years. They have now reached a breaking point. According to him, the whole province is buckling under these conditions with the western part of the Eastern Cape which has been greatly affected. In the eastern part of the province below average rainfall brought some relief. The situation is dire, says Stern. Based on the official report from the EC Department of Rural Development and Agrarian Reform, the following Districts and local Municipalities within the Province have been assessed as extremely and severely dry, expressed in percentages as follows: Sarah Baartman District 57,6 % with the Blue Crane Route Municipality at 77 % and the Dr Beyers Naude at LM at 65 %; Amatole District 40,1% with the Raymond Mhlaba LM at 85%; Chris Hani District 28,9% with the Inxuba Yethemba LM at 68%. Dam levels within the Districts indicate that within the three districts declared, the average number of major dam levels that have declined over the last twelve months are as follows: Sarah Baartman District and the Nelson Mandela Bay Metro 5 out of a total of 10 dams with 6 dams below 50%; Amatole District 12 out of a total of 14 dams with 8 dams below 50%; Chris Hani District 11 out of a total of 14 dams with 6 dams below 50%. According to estimates, livestock numbers decreased over the previous 12 months as follows: cattle by 55 000, sheep by 180 000 and goats by 72 000. With a third of the province in a critical position, more than 1 million cattle, 2.1 million sheep and 600 000 goats face an uncertain future. At least 30 million Rands worth of feed is going to be needed daily to prevent these animals from dying or having to be slaughtered.
